draft.title: Scatter graphs and correlation
card: A scatter graph plots two measures for many places. Each place is one dot, placed by its value on each measure.
the dots slope upward. As one measure rises, the other tends to rise too.
the dots slope downward. As one measure rises, the other tends to fall.
If the dots are scattered with no pattern, there is no correlation. A correlation shows a link, not a cause, because a third factor may affect both measures or the link may be chance.
draft.remember: A scatter graph shows whether two measures are linked. It does not show that one causes the other.

a.q: A scatter graph of 30 countries shows that the dots slope downward from left to right. What does this show about the two measures?
opts: One measure causes the other to fall
a.why: Dots that slope downward mean one measure tends to fall as the other rises, which is a negative correlation. A downward slope shows a link only, so saying one measure causes the other goes beyond what the graph shows.
a.clue: Look at the direction the dots slope.

b.q: A scatter graph of 40 Australian towns shows that towns with more ice cream sales also have more sunburn cases. What can be concluded?
opts: The measures rise together, but this does not prove a cause
Eating more ice cream causes people to get sunburnt
Sunburn cases cause ice cream sales to rise
The graph shows there is no link between the measures
b.why: The dots show a positive correlation, so the measures rise together. A correlation does not prove cause, and a third factor such as hot weather may affect both. Claiming ice cream causes sunburn treats a link as a cause.
b.clue: Could something else, such as the weather, affect both measures?

b.best: The measures rise together, but this does not prove a cause
